# Task 4: Building a Greenlight Risk Model

```{r}
#| label: task1-setup
#| include: false

library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 9))

focus_genres <- c(
  "Action", "Comedy", "Drama",
  "Horror", "Animation"
)

movies <- read_csv("data/movies.csv",
                   show_col_types = FALSE)

movies_clean <- movies |>
  filter(!is.na(release_year),
         release_year <= 2016) |>
  mutate(
    budget = if_else(budget < 10000, NA_real_, 
                     as.numeric(budget)),
    revenue = if_else(revenue <= 0, NA_real_,
                      as.numeric(revenue)),
    roi = if_else(
      !is.na(budget) & !is.na(revenue),
      revenue / budget,
      NA_real_
    ),
    budget_m = budget / 1e6,
    franchise_status = factor(
      franchise_status,
      levels = c("Original", "Franchise")
    )
  )

movies_focus <- movies_clean |>
  filter(primary_genre %in% focus_genres)
```


## Introduction

This analysis examines whether information available before production can help Meridian assess the risk of a film failing to recover its budget. We fitted *Frequentist and Bayesian logistic regression models* using genre, franchise status, production budget and crew size. The aim was to identify useful patterns in historical films and assess how these estimates might support greenlight decisions.

## Outcome and Predictor Definitions

```{r}
#| label: task4-outcome
#| include: false

# movies_clean was created in the shared setup chunk.

task4_data <- movies_clean |>
  mutate(
    flop = case_when(
      is.na(roi) ~ NA_integer_,
      roi < 1 ~ 1L,
      TRUE ~ 0L      
    )
  )

# Check the outcome categories.
task4_data |>
  count(flop, name = "number_of_films")
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-data-checks
#| include: false

# Check missing values in the selected predictors.
task4_data |>
  summarise(
    missing_genre = sum(is.na(primary_genre)),
    missing_franchise = sum(is.na(franchise_status)),
    missing_budget = sum(is.na(budget_m)),
    missing_crew = sum(is.na(crew_size))
  )

# Count films with complete information for modelling.
task4_data |>
  summarise(
    complete_model_cases = sum(
      complete.cases(
        flop,
        primary_genre,
        franchise_status,
        budget_m,
        crew_size
      )
    )
  )
```

A film was classified as a flop when its reported box-office revenue was lower than its production budget *(ROI < 1)*. Films with missing financial information were left unclassified rather than assumed to be successful or unsuccessful.

Of the 4,801 films examined, 3,214 had a known outcome, including 785 flops *(24.4%)*. After excluding observations with missing predictor information, *3,213 films remained for modelling*.

Logistic regression was chosen because the outcome is binary and the model estimates probabilities between zero and one. Genre, franchise status, budget and crew size were selected because these characteristics can be considered before production approval. Budget and crew size were expressed in units of $10 million and 10 people to make the results easier to interpret. Missing financial information may introduce *selection bias* if the films retained for modelling differ systematically from those excluded.

## Frequentist Logistic Regression

```{r}
#| label: task4-initial-model
#| include: false

task4_initial_model <- glm(
  flop ~ primary_genre + franchise_status + budget_m + crew_size,
  data = task4_data,
  family = binomial
)

summary(task4_initial_model)
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-genre-diagnostic
#| include: false

task4_data |>
  filter(!is.na(flop), !is.na(primary_genre)) |>
  count(primary_genre, flop) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from = flop,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0,
    names_prefix = "flop_"
  ) |>
  mutate(total = flop_0 + flop_1) |>
  arrange(total)
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-model-data
#| include: false

task4_model_data <- task4_data |>
  mutate(
    budget_10m = budget_m / 10,
    crew_10 = crew_size / 10
  ) |>
  filter(
    complete.cases(
      flop,
      primary_genre,
      franchise_status,
      budget_10m,
      crew_10
    )
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-frequentist-model
#| include: false

task4_frequentist <- glm(
  flop ~ primary_genre + franchise_status + budget_10m + crew_10,
  data = task4_model_data,
  family = binomial
)

summary(task4_frequentist)
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-frequentist-odds
#| include: false

odds_ratios <- exp(coef(task4_frequentist))

wald_intervals <- confint.default(task4_frequentist)

task4_odds_table <- data.frame(
  Predictor = names(odds_ratios),
  Odds_Ratio = odds_ratios,
  CI_Lower = exp(wald_intervals[, 1]),
  CI_Upper = exp(wald_intervals[, 2])
)

task4_odds_table |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    dplyr::across(
      c(Odds_Ratio, CI_Lower, CI_Upper),
      ~ round(.x, 3)
    )
  ) |>
  print(row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-frequentist-results
#| include: false

task4_odds_table |>
  dplyr::filter(
    Predictor %in% c(
      "franchise_statusFranchise",
      "budget_10m",
      "crew_10"
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    Predictor = dplyr::recode(
      Predictor,
      franchise_statusFranchise = "Franchise (vs original)",
      budget_10m = "Budget (+$10 million)",
      crew_10 = "Crew (+10 members)"
    ),
    dplyr::across(
      c(Odds_Ratio, CI_Lower, CI_Upper),
      ~ round(.x, 3)
    )
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Predictor",
      "Odds ratio",
      "95% CI lower",
      "95% CI upper"
    ),
    caption = "Selected frequentist logistic regression results"
  )
```
After adjusting for the other predictors, franchise films had substantially lower odds of flopping than original films *(OR = 0.224, 95% CI: 0.126–0.399)*. Each additional $10 million in budget was associated with *4.0% lower odds (OR = 0.960)*, while an additional 10 crew members was associated with *9.4% lower odds (OR = 0.906)*.

These relationships are associations, *not evidence* that larger budgets or crews directly reduce financial risk. The Foreign genre also contained only one film with a known outcome, leading to an unstable frequentist estimate.

## Bayesian Logistic Regression

```{r}
#| label: task4-bayesian-data-checks
#| include: false

# Outcome balance
task4_model_data |>
  dplyr::count(flop) |>
  dplyr::mutate(proportion = n / sum(n))

# Number of flops and non-flops in each genre
task4_model_data |>
  dplyr::group_by(primary_genre) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    films = dplyr::n(),
    flops = sum(flop == 1),
    non_flops = sum(flop == 0),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(films)

# Predictor scales
task4_model_data |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    budget_sd = sd(budget_10m),
    crew_sd = sd(crew_10),
    budget_median = median(budget_10m),
    crew_median = median(crew_10),
    budget_max = max(budget_10m),
    crew_max = max(crew_10)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-bayesian-predictors
#| include: false

task4_budget_mean <- mean(task4_model_data$budget_10m)
task4_budget_sd <- sd(task4_model_data$budget_10m)

task4_crew_mean <- mean(task4_model_data$crew_10)
task4_crew_sd <- sd(task4_model_data$crew_10)

task4_bayesian_data <- task4_model_data |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    budget_z = (budget_10m - task4_budget_mean) /
      task4_budget_sd,
    crew_z = (crew_10 - task4_crew_mean) /
      task4_crew_sd
  )

summary(task4_bayesian_data[, c("budget_z", "crew_z")])
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-bayesian-prior-check
#| include: false

set.seed(2420)

# Draw hypothetical coefficients from proposed priors
prior_intercept <- 2.5 * rt(10000, df = 3)
prior_franchise <- rnorm(10000, mean = 0, sd = 1.5)
prior_budget <- rnorm(10000, mean = 0, sd = 0.5)
prior_crew <- rnorm(10000, mean = 0, sd = 0.5)

# Illustrative profile: original film with average budget and crew
prior_prob_original <- plogis(prior_intercept)

# Illustrative profile: franchise film with average budget and crew
prior_prob_franchise <- plogis(
  prior_intercept + prior_franchise
)

# Summarise implied prior probabilities
rbind(
  Original = quantile(
    prior_prob_original,
    c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)
  ),
  Franchise = quantile(
    prior_prob_franchise,
    c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-bayesian-prior-comparison
#| include: false

set.seed(2420)

n_draws <- 10000

# Candidate intercept priors
intercept_a <- 2.5 * rt(n_draws, df = 3)
intercept_b <- rnorm(n_draws, mean = -1, sd = 1)

# Other coefficient priors
franchise_effect <- rnorm(n_draws, 0, 1.5)
budget_effect <- rnorm(n_draws, 0, 0.5)
crew_effect <- rnorm(n_draws, 0, 0.5)

# Representative profiles on standardised scales
prior_profiles <- data.frame(
  profile = c(
    "Original, average scale",
    "Franchise, average scale",
    "Original, higher scale"
  ),
  franchise = c(0, 1, 0),
  budget_z = c(0, 0, 1),
  crew_z = c(0, 0, 1)
)

# Function to summarise implied probabilities
check_prior <- function(intercept, prior_name) {

  results <- lapply(
    seq_len(nrow(prior_profiles)),
    function(i) {

      log_odds <- intercept +
        franchise_effect * prior_profiles$franchise[i] +
        budget_effect * prior_profiles$budget_z[i] +
        crew_effect * prior_profiles$crew_z[i]

      probabilities <- plogis(log_odds)

      data.frame(
        prior = prior_name,
        profile = prior_profiles$profile[i],
        lower = quantile(probabilities, 0.025),
        median = median(probabilities),
        upper = quantile(probabilities, 0.975)
      )
    }
  )

  dplyr::bind_rows(results)
}

prior_comparison <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  check_prior(intercept_a, "A: Student-t(3, 0, 2.5)"),
  check_prior(intercept_b, "B: Normal(-1, 1)")
)

print(prior_comparison)
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-bayesian-final-priors
#| include: false

# Design matrix for Bayesian logistic regression
task4_formula <- flop ~ primary_genre + franchise_status +
  budget_z + crew_z

task4_X <- model.matrix(
  task4_formula,
  data = task4_bayesian_data
)

task4_y <- task4_bayesian_data$flop

# Prior standard deviations for regression coefficients
task4_prior_sd <- rep(1.5, ncol(task4_X))
names(task4_prior_sd) <- colnames(task4_X)

task4_prior_sd["(Intercept)"] <- 1
task4_prior_sd["budget_z"] <- 0.5
task4_prior_sd["crew_z"] <- 0.5

# Prior means
task4_prior_mean <- rep(0, ncol(task4_X))
names(task4_prior_mean) <- colnames(task4_X)

task4_prior_mean["(Intercept)"] <- -1

# Log-posterior = log-likelihood + log-prior
task4_log_posterior <- function(beta) {

  eta <- drop(task4_X %*% beta)

  # Numerically stable Bernoulli log-likelihood
  log_likelihood <- sum(
    task4_y * eta -
      (pmax(eta, 0) + log1p(exp(-abs(eta))))
  )

  log_prior <- sum(
    dnorm(
      beta,
      mean = task4_prior_mean,
      sd = task4_prior_sd,
      log = TRUE
    )
  )

  log_likelihood + log_prior
}
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-bayesian-fit
#| include: false

# Locate a suitable starting point for Metropolis sampling
task4_mode <- optim(
  par = task4_prior_mean,
  fn = function(beta) -task4_log_posterior(beta),
  method = "BFGS",
  hessian = TRUE,
  control = list(maxit = 2000)
)

print(task4_mode$convergence)

# Estimate the proposal covariance
task4_proposal_cov <- solve(task4_mode$hessian)

# Run four Metropolis-Hastings chains
set.seed(2420)

task4_mh_chains <- lapply(1:4, function(chain) {

  starting_values <- as.numeric(
    MASS::mvrnorm(
      1,
      mu = task4_mode$par,
      Sigma = task4_proposal_cov
    )
  )

  chain_result <- MCMCpack::MCMCmetrop1R(
    fun = task4_log_posterior,
    theta.init = starting_values,
    V = task4_proposal_cov,
    tune = 0.4,
    burnin = 4000,
    mcmc = 12000,
    thin = 1,
    logfun = TRUE,
    verbose = 0
  )

  colnames(chain_result) <- colnames(task4_X)

  chain_result
})

task4_mh_chains <- do.call(
  coda::mcmc.list,
  task4_mh_chains
)
saveRDS(task4_mh_chains, "task4_mh_fit.rds")

# Combine the four chains into a matrix of posterior draws
task4_mh_draws <- as.matrix(task4_mh_chains)
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-bayesian-diagnostics
#| include: false

# Check agreement between the four chains
task4_rhat <- coda::gelman.diag(
  task4_mh_chains,
  multivariate = FALSE
)

# Check effective sample sizes
task4_ess <- coda::effectiveSize(task4_mh_chains)

print(task4_rhat)
cat("Minimum ESS:", round(min(task4_ess), 1), "\n")
cat(
  "Maximum upper R-hat:",
  round(max(task4_rhat$psrf[, 2]), 3),
  "\n"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-task4-bayesian-results
#| include: false
#| tbl-cap: "Selected Bayesian logistic regression estimates with 95% credible intervals."

task4_bayesian_results <- data.frame(
  Predictor = c(
    "Franchise (vs original)",
    "Budget (+$10 million)",
    "Crew (+10 members)"
  ),
  Median_OR = c(
    median(exp(task4_mh_draws[, "franchise_statusFranchise"])),
    median(exp(task4_mh_draws[, "budget_z"] / task4_budget_sd)),
    median(exp(task4_mh_draws[, "crew_z"] / task4_crew_sd))
  ),
  Lower = c(
    quantile(exp(task4_mh_draws[, "franchise_statusFranchise"]), 0.025),
    quantile(exp(task4_mh_draws[, "budget_z"] / task4_budget_sd), 0.025),
    quantile(exp(task4_mh_draws[, "crew_z"] / task4_crew_sd), 0.025)
  ),
  Upper = c(
    quantile(exp(task4_mh_draws[, "franchise_statusFranchise"]), 0.975),
    quantile(exp(task4_mh_draws[, "budget_z"] / task4_budget_sd), 0.975),
    quantile(exp(task4_mh_draws[, "crew_z"] / task4_crew_sd), 0.975)
  )
)

task4_bayesian_results |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    `Median odds ratio (95% CrI)` = sprintf(
      "%.3f (%.3f–%.3f)", Median_OR, Lower, Upper
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(Predictor, `Median odds ratio (95% CrI)`) |>
  knitr::kable(row.names = FALSE)
```

**Bayesian findings and limitations**
The Bayesian model used the same predictors, with budget and crew size standardised before estimation. We compared candidate priors and selected a *Normal(−1, 1)* intercept prior, Normal(0, 1.5) priors for genre and franchise coefficients, and Normal(0, 0.5) priors for standardised budget and crew coefficients. These choices provided some regularisation while allowing uncertainty in the effects.

We estimated the posterior using four *Metropolis–Hastings chains*, with 4,000 burn-in iterations and 12,000 retained draws per chain. A proposal *tuning factor of 0.4* was used to control the size of proposed moves. Acceptance rates were approximately *35.5%–36.6%*, the minimum effective sample size was 522, and the maximum upper *R-hat was 1.012*. These checks suggest reasonable sampling stability, although they cannot rule out model misspecification.

## Model Comparison

```{r}
#| label: task4-model-comparison-data
#| include: false

# Frequentist estimates
frequentist_coefs <- coef(task4_frequentist)
frequentist_ci <- confint.default(task4_frequentist)

predictors <- c(
  "franchise_statusFranchise",
  "budget_10m",
  "crew_10"
)


# Convert Bayesian coefficients to comparable odds ratios
bayesian_or_draws <- cbind(
  Franchise = exp(
    task4_mh_draws[, "franchise_statusFranchise"]
  ),
  Budget = exp(
    task4_mh_draws[, "budget_z"] / task4_budget_sd
  ),
  Crew = exp(
    task4_mh_draws[, "crew_z"] / task4_crew_sd
  )
)

# Summarise posterior odds ratios
bayesian_medians <- apply(bayesian_or_draws, 2, median)
bayesian_lower <- apply(bayesian_or_draws, 2, quantile, 0.025)
bayesian_upper <- apply(bayesian_or_draws, 2, quantile, 0.975)

comparison <- data.frame(
  Predictor = c("Franchise", "Budget (+$10m)", "Crew (+10)"),
  Frequentist_OR = exp(frequentist_coefs[predictors]),
  Frequentist_Lower = exp(frequentist_ci[predictors, 1]),
  Frequentist_Upper = exp(frequentist_ci[predictors, 2]),
  Bayesian_OR = as.numeric(bayesian_medians),
  Bayesian_Lower = as.numeric(bayesian_lower),
  Bayesian_Upper = as.numeric(bayesian_upper)
)

print(comparison)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-task4-model-comparison
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Frequentist and Bayesian odds ratios with 95% uncertainty intervals."

comparison_display <- data.frame(
  Predictor = comparison$Predictor,
  Frequentist = sprintf(
    "%.3f (%.3f–%.3f)",
    comparison$Frequentist_OR,
    comparison$Frequentist_Lower,
    comparison$Frequentist_Upper
  ),
  Bayesian = sprintf(
    "%.3f (%.3f–%.3f)",
    comparison$Bayesian_OR,
    comparison$Bayesian_Lower,
    comparison$Bayesian_Upper
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  comparison_display,
  col.names = c(
    "Predictor",
    "Frequentist OR (95% CI)",
    "Bayesian OR (95% CrI)"
  ),
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-posterior-probability
#| include: false

# Posterior probability that franchise status reduces flop odds
franchise_draws <- task4_mh_draws[, "franchise_statusFranchise"]

prob_franchise_negative <- mean(franchise_draws < 0)

print(prob_franchise_negative)
```

The frequentist and Bayesian logistic regression models both approaches gave *similar results*. For franchise status, the frequentist odds ratio was 0.224 (95% CI: 0.126–0.399), compared with a Bayesian posterior median odds ratio of *0.238 (95% credible interval: 0.132–0.390)*. Budget and crew size also showed similar associations across the two models.

The intervals have different interpretations: frequentist confidence intervals describe the long-run coverage of the estimation procedure, whereas Bayesian credible intervals describe uncertainty about the coefficients given the data and priors.*More than 99.9%* of retained posterior draws indicated lower flop odds for franchise films, after accounting for the other predictors.

The Bayesian prior reduced instability in sparse categories, but the *Foreign genre remained too poorly represented* for a reliable conclusion. 

## Classification Performance

```{r}
#| label: task4-classification-predictions
#| include: false

# Predict flop probabilities using the frequentist model
task4_predicted_prob <- predict(
  task4_frequentist,
  newdata = task4_model_data,
  type = "response"
)

# Classify films using a 50% probability threshold
task4_predicted_class <- ifelse(
  task4_predicted_prob >= 0.5,
  1L,
  0L
)

# Compare predicted and actual outcomes
task4_confusion <- table(
  Actual = factor(task4_model_data$flop, levels = c(0, 1)),
  Predicted = factor(task4_predicted_class, levels = c(0, 1))
)

print(task4_confusion)
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-classification-metrics
#| include: false

# Extract the four confusion matrix counts
task4_tn <- task4_confusion["0", "0"]
task4_fp <- task4_confusion["0", "1"]
task4_fn <- task4_confusion["1", "0"]
task4_tp <- task4_confusion["1", "1"]

# Calculate classification performance
task4_accuracy <- (task4_tp + task4_tn) / sum(task4_confusion)

task4_sensitivity <- task4_tp / (task4_tp + task4_fn)

task4_specificity <- task4_tn / (task4_tn + task4_fp)

task4_precision <- if (
  task4_tp + task4_fp > 0
) {
  task4_tp / (task4_tp + task4_fp)
} else {
  NA_real_
}

# Summarise performance
task4_metrics <- data.frame(
  Metric = c(
    "Accuracy",
    "Sensitivity (flops)",
    "Specificity (non-flops)",
    "Precision (predicted flops)"
  ),
  Value = c(
    task4_accuracy,
    task4_sensitivity,
    task4_specificity,
    task4_precision
  )
)

print(task4_metrics)
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-threshold-comparison
#| include: false

# Compare classification results at two probability thresholds
task4_threshold_metrics <- function(threshold) {

  predicted <- ifelse(task4_predicted_prob >= threshold, 1L, 0L)

  actual <- task4_model_data$flop

  tp <- sum(predicted == 1 & actual == 1)
  tn <- sum(predicted == 0 & actual == 0)
  fp <- sum(predicted == 1 & actual == 0)
  fn <- sum(predicted == 0 & actual == 1)

  data.frame(
    Threshold = threshold,
    Accuracy = (tp + tn) / length(actual),
    Sensitivity = tp / (tp + fn),
    Specificity = tn / (tn + fp),
    Precision = tp / (tp + fp),
    Flops_Detected = tp,
    Flops_Missed = fn
  )
}

task4_threshold_results <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  task4_threshold_metrics(0.50),
  task4_threshold_metrics(0.30)
)

print(task4_threshold_results)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-task4-classification-performance
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "In-sample classification performance at two probability thresholds."

task4_performance_display <- task4_threshold_results |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    Threshold = paste0(round(Threshold * 100), "%"),
    dplyr::across(
      c(Accuracy, Sensitivity, Specificity, Precision),
      ~ sprintf("%.1f%%", .x * 100)
    )
  )

knitr::kable(
  task4_performance_display,
  col.names = c(
    "Threshold",
    "Accuracy",
    "Sensitivity",
    "Specificity",
    "Precision",
    "Flops detected",
    "Flops missed"
  ),
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-task4-confusion-matrix
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "In-sample confusion matrix at the 30% threshold."

task4_confusion_display <- table(
  Actual = factor(
    task4_model_data$flop,
    levels = c(0, 1),
    labels = c("Non-flop", "Flop")
  ),
  Predicted = factor(
    ifelse(task4_predicted_prob >= 0.30, 1, 0),
    levels = c(0, 1),
    labels = c("Non-flop", "Flop")
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  as.data.frame.matrix(task4_confusion_display),
  col.names = c("Predicted non-flop", "Predicted flop")
)
```

**Classification performance**

At the standard 50% threshold, the frequentist model achieved *75.6% accuracy but* identified only 5 of the 784 actual flops *(sensitivity 0.6%)*. This illustrates why accuracy alone can be misleading when non-flops are more common.

Lowering the threshold to 30% increased sensitivity to *43.1%*, identifying 338 flops. However, specificity fell to 74.2%, precision was 35.0%, and *627 non-flops* were *incorrectly flagged*. Overall accuracy decreased to 66.6%.

For Meridian, a lower threshold may be more useful for screening projects when missing a potential flop is costly. However, it also increases unnecessary reviews, and 30% should not be treated as an optimal threshold. These figures were calculated on the *training sample*, so performance on new films remains uncertain.

## Hypothetical Film Pitches

```{r}
#| label: task4-hypothetical-pitches
#| include: false

task4_pitches <- data.frame(
  Pitch = c(
    "Platform Zero",
    "The Meridian Protocol: Black Tide",
    "The Things We Never Recorded"
  ),
  primary_genre = c("Horror", "Action", "Drama"),
  franchise_status = c("Original", "Franchise", "Original"),
  budget_10m = c(0.9, 8.5, 1.8),
  crew_10 = c(2.4, 9, 3.8)
)

# Keep the same categories as the fitted model
task4_pitches$primary_genre <- factor(
  task4_pitches$primary_genre,
  levels = sort(unique(task4_model_data$primary_genre))
)

task4_pitches$franchise_status <- factor(
  task4_pitches$franchise_status,
  levels = levels(task4_model_data$franchise_status)
)

# Apply the standardisation used in the Bayesian model
task4_pitches <- task4_pitches |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    budget_z = (budget_10m - task4_budget_mean) / task4_budget_sd,
    crew_z = (crew_10 - task4_crew_mean) / task4_crew_sd
  )

print(task4_pitches)
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-pitch-predictions
#| include: false

# Build the predictor matrix using the fitted model's columns
task4_pitch_X <- model.matrix(
  ~ primary_genre + franchise_status + budget_z + crew_z,
  data = task4_pitches
)

# Ensure the columns match the Bayesian model
task4_pitch_X <- task4_pitch_X[, colnames(task4_mh_draws), drop = FALSE]

# Predicted flop probability for every posterior draw and pitch
task4_pitch_prob_draws <- plogis(
  task4_mh_draws %*% t(task4_pitch_X)
)

# Summarise the posterior probabilities
task4_pitch_results <- data.frame(
  Pitch = task4_pitches$Pitch,
  Median_Probability = apply(task4_pitch_prob_draws, 2, median),
  Lower_95 = apply(task4_pitch_prob_draws, 2, quantile, probs = 0.025),
  Upper_95 = apply(task4_pitch_prob_draws, 2, quantile, probs = 0.975)
)

print(task4_pitch_results)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-task4-pitch-predictions
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Bayesian predicted flop probabilities and 95% credible intervals for three hypothetical pitches."

task4_pitch_display <- task4_pitch_results |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    `Flop probability` = sprintf("%.1f%%", Median_Probability * 100),
    `95% credible interval` = sprintf(
      "%.1f%%–%.1f%%",
      Lower_95 * 100,
      Upper_95 * 100
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(
    Pitch,
    `Flop probability`,
    `95% credible interval`
  )

knitr::kable(task4_pitch_display, row.names = FALSE)
```

### Hypothetical Film Pitches and Greenlight recommendations

Three fictional pitches were assessed using the Bayesian model. Their estimated flop probabilities and 95% credible intervals reflect uncertainty in the model's predictions.

*The Meridian Protocol: Black Tide* — *Conditional greenlight*. This $85 million franchise action film had the lowest predicted flop probability at 4.7% (95% CrI: 2.7%–7.9%). Its relatively low estimated risk supports further consideration, but the large budget makes a separate revenue and potential-loss assessment important before approval.

*Platform Zero* — Conditional greenlight. This $9 million original horror film had a predicted flop probability of 16.0% (95% CrI: 11.2%–22.2%). Its smaller budget limits the initial financial commitment. Approval should depend on whether the expected audience and distribution arrangements support the investment.

*The Things We Never Recorded* — *Hold for review*. This $18 million original drama had the highest estimated flop probability at 28.8% (95% CrI: 25.6%–32.6%). The project would benefit from reviewing its budget and expected revenue before Meridian commits to production.

A lower flop probability does not necessarily imply a higher expected financial return, since the model does not estimate the size of potential profits or losses.


## Summary for the Head of Production

The models provide Meridian with an initial way to compare financial risk across film proposals using information available before production. Franchise status, budget and crew size were associated with flop outcomes in the historical data, but the *results should not be interpreted as causal*.

The main limitations are missing financial records, limited observations for some genres and the absence of important commercial factors such as marketing, audience demand and distribution. The classification results were also assessed on the same data used to fit the model, so *performance on future productions is not established*.

Meridian should therefore use these predictions to identify projects requiring closer financial review, alongside revenue forecasts and professional judgement, *rather than as automatic greenlight decision*s.
